title: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate→Verify→Repair vs LLM‑Only NetOps Suggestions: A Null Result on a Deterministic Synthetic Task Pool
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop) that measured the marginal effect of inserting a deterministic verifier+repair step (generate→verify→repair, G→V→R) versus accepting an LLM suggestion directly for intent→configuration NetOps tasks. Using a deterministic task generator and a deterministic validator, K=200 tasks were selected via a reproducible SHA‑256 sorting rule. A single shared generator output per task (shared_initial_generation) was evaluated in both arms. Requested_model = gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256: 1acce92558ed...). Observed primary outcome: baseline = 200/200 validator‑compliant applies; guarded = 200/200; paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; paired bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.00,0.00]. The repair pathway was never invoked. All preregistered artifacts, raw traces, scoring records, and analysis artifacts are archived with SHA‑256 hashes to permit exact replay (raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 3dfbe1b6...). We interpret the null as a ceiling case for this specific task/model/validator regime and provide operational and methodological guidance for future confirmatory evaluations that aim to demonstrate verifier and repair utility in more failure‑rich settings.

sections.introduction:
Automating the translation from high‑level operator intent into concrete device configuration promises to accelerate change velocity in modern networks. However, erroneous or out‑of‑sequence configuration changes can cause immediate operational regressions (reachability breaks, service loss). A standard mitigation architecture is generate→verify→repair (G→V→R): let a stochastic generator (LLM) propose candidate configuration commands, run a deterministic verifier/emulator against the candidate to detect violations of workflow constraints or safety properties, and, when violations occur, apply an automated repair module to produce a corrected candidate. Prior system papers and benchmarks propose G→V→R as a pragmatic path to operational trustworthiness, yet the measurable marginal benefit of verifier+repair depends on generator error rates, validator coverage, and the task distribution.
We designed a preregistered paired experiment that isolates the verifier’s marginal effect by holding the generator output identical across arms (shared_initial_generation). This removes generator variability as a confound and produces a clean paired estimand: the within‑task difference in regression‑causing change rate (guarded minus baseline). Our preregistration (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop; SHA‑256 a6d73a5c...) prespecified deterministic task selection, validator semantics, analysis plan, multiplicity handling, and auditing artifacts. This paper reports the full artifact‑grounded execution, the confirmatory statistics, and an interpretation of the observed degenerate null result where the verifier never observed a failing candidate.
sections.related_work: Recent literature spans three converging strands: LLM‑assisted configuration synthesis and intent translation for NetOps; generate→validate→repair pipelines and formal verification tools for network configurations; and agentic orchestration frameworks that mediate model outputs with deterministic checkers. Benchmarks such as Cornetto and position papers advocating translation‑plus‑solver architectures emphasise that reliable automation requires deterministic checks and that verification can catch regressions introduced by model hallucination. Other work argues for confining models to translation/encoding tasks while relying on solvers/SMT engines for reasoning. Our study complements this body by providing a preregistered, paired causal estimate under a deterministic synthetic pool and by releasing exact per‑episode validator traces and provider call logs to enable replay and scrutiny. The included nearest‑work leads (e.g., Cornetto and related verification/transformation proposals) were used to define task difficulty patterns and validator checks that shaped the preregistered task generator and validator coverage matrix.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration. We preregistered the complete experimental design and analysis plan (study_id=cand-002-gvr-loop; preregistration SHA‑256: a6d73a5c...). The primary confirmatory hypothesis H1 expected that G→V→R (guarded) would reduce regression‑causing changes relative to LLM‑only (baseline). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Power plan: target absolute reduction 0.08 assuming baseline regression rate ≈ 0.20 (two‑sided α=0.05, power=0.80); sensitivity checks across baseline values were preregistered.
Task construction and deterministic sampling. Tasks were derived from a deterministic synthetic intent pool generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Inclusion required preregistered validator coverage. To avoid human selection bias we sorted intents by SHA‑256(intent_string) and selected the first K=200 unique tasks after automated filtering; all selection decisions and exclusion reasons were logged (execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 f1d447b7...). Task payloads include initial_state, expected_final_state, explicit workflow constraints (e.g., "must shut interface before MTU change"), and a canonical required_sequence used by the validator to check ordering properties. Representative manifest entries are archived and reproduced in the artifact bundle.
Shared initial generation and paired design. For each selected intent we issued a single generator call (shared_initial_generation) requesting a candidate configuration candidate_c. The baseline arm accepts candidate_c as the suggested apply; the guarded arm first runs deterministic_netops_validator_v5 on candidate_c, and may invoke a single preregistered repair call if and only if the validator reports violations (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Critically, shared_initial_generation isolates the verifier marginal effect by fixing generator output across arms; it also prevents the generator from receiving verifier feedback (see Discussion). Model budget and provider auditing: requested_model = gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256: 1acce9255...), maximum_model_calls = 400; because the single shared generation served both arms actual model_calls_used = 200. Provider calls and per‑call hashes were archived to detect unintended caching or cross‑condition reuse; no cross‑condition cache reuse was observed (deterministic_reconciliation.json).
Validator and scoring semantics. deterministic_netops_validator_v5 parses candidate text, maps commands to structured field changes, and enforces workflow invariants (group minimum‑up constraints, "must_be_down_for_fields", protected interface constraints). Scoring rule used for the confirmatory outcome was full_intent_constraint_validation — a binary valid flag (validator.valid). Scorer outputs include normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, final_state snapshot, and violation codes; representative scoring traces are in execution/scoring/*.json with SHA‑256s recorded in the manifest. Repair behavior (when invoked) was to issue a single constrained repair prompt to the same requested_model and revalidate once; repair traces would be archived similarly. The preregistration required all repairs, retries, and exclusions to be logged; in this run, repair_applied==false for every guarded episode.
Statistical analysis. Confirmatory test: exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary outcomes (validator pass/fail) with paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). Secondary estimands (time‑to‑deploy, model calls per successful apply) were preregistered; because repairs were never invoked these secondary outcomes did not discriminate arms but are reported in execution accounting. Analysis code and logs are archived (analysis/* with SHA‑256 hashes).

Planned episodes = 400 (2 × K for K=200 paired tasks); completed episodes = 400; failed episodes = 0. Model calls used = 200 (one shared generator call per task), maximum_model_calls permitted = 400. Paired contingency table (guarded × baseline): n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 7bc1bd2a...). Paired estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.00. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) = [0.00,0.00] (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl).
Repair and cost accounting. The guarded repair path was never invoked: repair_applied=false for all guarded episodes. Consequently the guarded arm consumed no additional model calls beyond the shared initial generation. Per‑task diagnostics recorded parsed_command_count and observed_touched_field_count to measure task complexity (e.g., task-000003 parsed_command_count=6, difficulty=hard). These diagnostics are archived and enable external auditors to re-evaluate validator coverage or to replay emulation snapshots.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation: ceiling case vs constructive evidence. The observed degenerate null — perfect validator compliance in both arms and zero repair invocations — is a valid experimental outcome: under the selected task pool, generator, and deterministic validator, every shared generator candidate satisfied the preregistered validation constraints. This outcome demonstrates a ceiling regime in which the verifier could not affect the binary apply outcome because there was nothing to correct. The result does not imply verifiers are universally unnecessary; rather it documents one reproducible condition in which the generator proposals already met validator expectations.
Why this happened (artifact‑grounded explanation). Three artifact‑grounded factors explain the ceiling: (1) deterministic task generator filtered to intents already covered by the validator, biasing the sample toward validator‑compatible intents; (2) the requested_model (gpt-5-mini, configured as recorded) produced candidates that respected the signed workflow constraints for these synthetic intents; and (3) the shared_initial_generation paired design prevents iterative generator adaptation to validator feedback (the generator never received verifier signals, so downstream repair opportunities would only arise if the initial candidate failed validation). All three elements are explicit in the preregistration and execution manifest and can be verified via the archived task_manifest.jsonl, provider traces, and scoring logs.
Design lessons and recommendations. To demonstrate verifier/repair utility in a confirmatory paired format researchers should (artifact‑grounded): (A) construct a task bank that intentionally samples near validator boundary cases or historical failure instances so baseline generator error rate is nontrivial; (B) evaluate multiple generator strengths including weaker models to increase baseline failure probability; (C) consider interactive generator–verifier designs where the generator may adapt to validator feedback (this changes the estimand); (D) ensure validator coverage is measured and reported per intent so sample selection is transparent. Our experiment’s artifacts (task manifests, validator coverage matrix) illustrate how to operationalize these recommendations reproducibly.
Threats to validity. Internal validity: preserved through deterministic sampling, seeded generation, and cryptographic hashing of artifacts (all hashes included in execution manifest). Construct validity: hinges on whether validator.valid corresponds to operationally meaningful regressions—this depends on validator fidelity; we archived full validator_final_state snapshots so external evaluators may judge fidelity. External validity: limited because we used a single model (gpt-5-mini), synthetic deterministic tasks, and the deterministic validator; production distributions with vendor idiosyncrasies, partial observability, and telemetry noise are not represented. Conclusion validity: the preregistered power assumption (baseline failure ≈ 0.20) was violated by the observed baseline = 1.0; in such cases power calculations are moot and exact paired tests plus bootstrap CIs (reported here) provide appropriate inference.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired comparison of G→V→R versus LLM‑only acceptance on 200 deterministically sampled NetOps tasks. Under the chosen task/model/validator regime the verifier had no marginal effect: both arms produced 200/200 validator‑compliant applies; paired difference = 0.00; McNemar p = 1.00; bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00,0.00]. The repair loop was never invoked. This ceiling case demonstrates that a confirmatory demonstration of verifier/repair benefit requires a sample and generator regime with nontrivial baseline failure rates or an interactive design that allows generator adaptation. We release the complete artifact bundle (preregistration, provider traces, responses, scoring, execution manifest, analysis artifacts) with SHA‑256 hashes to enable exact replay and to serve as a template for future preregistered evaluations aimed at quantifying verifier value in realistic operational distributions.

limitations: Single‑model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) — results do not generalize to other LLMs without further experiments.
Synthetic deterministic task pool and deterministic sampling — external validity to production intents, vendor diversity, and noisy telemetry is limited.
Primary outcome depends on deterministic_netops_validator_v5 fidelity; construct validity is tied to validator coverage of real regression modes.
Ceiling effect: observed baseline success = 100% eliminated ability to demonstrate verifier/repair benefit under this design and task sample.
Residual contamination (undetectable training‑data overlap) cannot be fully excluded despite hashing and logging; contamination_summary.csv recorded no flagged items for this run.
